title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: Brute force to optimized: unmemoized recursive match/drop exploration versus a 2D bottom-up DP grid.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence (a sequence appearing in both strings in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguous); return 0 if there is none.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","text1, text2"],["Output","Length of their longest common subsequence"],["Goal","dp[i][j] = LCS length of text1's first i characters and text2's first j characters"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 characters each"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Longest common subsequence between two strings\"","The classic 2D string-matching DP: comparing the LAST characters of both prefixes decides whether to extend diagonally or take the best of dropping one character from either string"]]}

blocks.text: Define dp[i][j] as the LCS length between the first i characters of text1 and the first j characters of text2. If the LAST characters of these two prefixes MATCH, they can both be included in the subsequence, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. If they do NOT match, at least one of the two last characters cannot be part of the optimal subsequence ending here, so dp[i][j] is the BETTER of dropping the last character of text1 (dp[i-1][j]) or dropping the last character of text2 (dp[i][j-1]).

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Shared Storyline Between Two Different Retellings
blocks.text: Picture comparing two different retellings of a story, looking for the longest sequence of shared plot points that appear in the same order in both (though other details may differ or be skipped). If both retellings' latest plot point matches, it extends a shared storyline found earlier; if not, the best shared storyline so far is whichever retelling, with its very last point dropped, gives a longer match.

blocks.caption: Matching last characters extend the diagonal LCS by 1; otherwise take the best of dropping one character from either string

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: dp[i][0] and dp[0][j] are always 0, since an empty string shares no subsequence with anything.

Observation 2: If text1[i-1] equals text2[j-1] (the last characters of the current prefixes), this shared character can extend whatever LCS existed between the prefixes BEFORE it, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.

Observation 3: If they do NOT match, the LCS at this point cannot use BOTH of these last characters together, so the best answer is the larger of dp[i-1][j] (drop text1's last character) and dp[i][j-1] (drop text2's last character).

Observation 4: Filling this 2D grid row by row (or column by column) builds the answer up to dp[m][n], the final result.
This leads to a 2D bottom-up DP grid, comparing characters and either extending diagonally or taking the better of the top and left neighbors.
Recursively try including or excluding characters from both strings, without memoization, exploring every possible way to align a common subsequence.
Why the code is written this way

items: Recursively exploring match/drop choices directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the same (i, j) sub-positions repeatedly across different recursive paths, costing exponential time; a 2D DP grid computes each sub-position exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to (m+n)) without memoization.
Space: O(m+n) recursion depth.
Limitation: a 2D DP grid computes each (i, j) sub-position exactly once, reusing smaller sub-positions directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a (m+1) by (n+1) DP grid, with the first row and column all 0. For i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n: if text1[i-1] equals text2[j-1], set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; otherwise, set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Return dp[m][n].
Use a 2D bottom-up DP grid, extending diagonally on a match or taking the better of the top and left neighbors otherwise.

blocks.text: Comparing the last characters of the two current prefixes at every (i, j) correctly captures whether a shared character can extend a previously found common subsequence (diagonal case), or whether the best answer must come from ignoring the last character of one string or the other (the max of the top and left neighbors); building this bottom-up guarantees all smaller sub-positions a cell depends on are already correctly computed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m times n).
Space: O(m times n), reducible to O(min(m,n)) using a rolling row.

blocks.text: Longest Common Subsequence is the foundational two-string comparison DP problem, underlying diff tools, DNA sequence alignment, and many other string-matching techniques.

items: Confusing subsequence (order preserved, not necessarily contiguous) with substring (must be contiguous), leading to an entirely different, incorrect algorithm.
Off-by-one errors when indexing text1[i-1] and text2[j-1] versus the DP grid's 1-indexed dimensions.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "matching last characters extend diagonally, otherwise take the best of dropping one character from either string" is the exact recurrence to communicate clearly and quickly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "longest common subsequence between two strings", think: a 2D DP grid comparing characters, extending diagonally on a match.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs O(2^(m+n)); the 2D DP grid costs O(m times n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: 2D bottom-up dynamic programming comparing two strings character by character.
Core Idea: matching characters extend the diagonal by 1; mismatched characters take the best of dropping one character from either string.
Time: O(2^(m+n)) for the brute force, O(m times n) for the DP approach.
Space: O(m+n) recursion depth for the brute force, O(m times n) (reducible to O(min(m,n))) for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: subsequence means order-preserved, not necessarily contiguous, a key distinction from substring problems.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, foundational medium-level DP problem.
One line memory trick: match extends the diagonal; mismatch takes the better neighbor.
